subject: english-language
title: Lakoff and the Deficit Model
welcome_lead: Robin Lakoff opened the field. Her 1975 catalogue of women's language features sparked decades of debate.
meta_desc: Robin Lakoff's 1975 deficit model and women's language features at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have audited the deficit model — provocative, foundational and rightly contested.

concepts.def: Robin Lakoff (Language and Woman's Place, 1975) argued women's language showed features of powerlessness — hedges, tags, super-polite forms.
Devices like 'sort of', 'I think' that soften assertion; Lakoff listed them as a female feature.
Phrases like 'isn't it?' appended to statements; Lakoff associated them with female speech and uncertainty.
Lakoff's term for evaluative items (lovely, divine) marked as feminine.
Use of more formal grammar than required, claimed by Lakoff as a marker of female speech.
Subsequent research (O'Barr & Atkins 1980) reframed Lakoff's features as 'powerless language', not female language.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Lakoff listed roughly ten features she said characterised women's language: hedges, tag questions, super-polite forms, empty adjectives, intensifiers (so), italics, hypercorrect grammar, indirect requests, lack of humour and apologies.

The collective effect, she argued, was to project tentativeness — a deficit relative to male assertiveness.

Studying US courtroom witnesses, O'Barr and Atkins (1980) found the same features in low-status male witnesses. They renamed it powerless language.

The features index status, not biology — an early devastating critique of essentialism.

Lakoff drew largely on introspection and media examples. Later quantitative work (Holmes) found tag questions often perform facilitative functions, inviting participation rather than signalling doubt.
